Position: LLM performance on “reasoning” tasks is
best explained as context-directed extrapolation from
training-data priors (as opposed to stochastic parroting
or human-like advanced reasoning), and the community
should adopt evaluation controls that explicitly separate
remembering/understanding from Apply-level generali-

the basis for how LLMs achieve this is central to several
key considerations, including the continued development of

5. Conclusions & Call to Action
The perception that LLMs display unpredictable, emergent
reasoning has fueled claims about consciousness or agency
and has motivated a growing safety discourse (Long et al.,
2024). While it is prudent to prepare for a range of AI
advances, we argue that near-term research and evaluation
should be guided by the more empirically grounded view
that current LLM behaviour is best characterised as context-
directed extrapolation from training priors, including priors
shaped by post-training processes such as instruction tuning
and GDPO. This framing reduces the need to attribute intent
or deception to models: many “strategic” behaviours can be
induced by prompts that elicit particular priors rather than
reflecting intrinsic agency (Hagendorff, 2024; Phuong et al.,
2024; Scheurer et al., 2024; Keeling et al., 2024).
Viewing LLMs through the lens of context-directed extrapo-
lation clarifies several otherwise puzzling phenomena. First,
it explains why carefully curated prompts are often nec-
essary: the prompt acts as a selection mechanism that de-
termines whether the model activates task-relevant priors.
Second, it explains why LLMs can fail on counterfactuals
(even simple ones that children solve) while succeeding
on superficially “harder” problems. For example, conflict-
ing outcomes on ToM evaluations (e.g., failures onfaux
pastasks versus success on the Sally–Anne test (Baron-
Cohen et al., 1985)) are consistent with context-dependent
activation of different priors, rather than a stable, unitary

Title:
Neither Stochastic Parroting nor AGI: LLMs Solve Tasks through Context-Directed Extrapolation from Training Data Priors
Authors:
Harish Tayyar Madabushi
,
Melissa Torgbi
,
Claire Bonial
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract:
This position paper argues that many behaviours framed as either "stochastic parroting" or "advanced reasoning" are better explained as context-directed extrapolation from training-data priors, and that ML and NLP research communities would benefit from evaluations that distinguish remembering and basic extrapolation from genuine application-level generalisation. Our central contribution is an actionable evaluation checklist and design patterns that make these distinctions testable in practice. Our framework posits that LLMs extrapolate from training data priors while using context to guide the model to the appropriate priors; we call this "context-directed extrapolation." Specifically, this context direction is achieved through examples in base models, leading to in-context learning, while instruction tuning allows analogous task specification via prompts rather than explicit examples. We argue that adopting this more realistic framework and controls for improving evaluation would better calibrate claims about LLM "reasoning," refocus research on how LLM performance interacts with training data and generalisability to out-of-domain tasks, and reduce miscalibration in deployment and policy decisions.
